strengths: Addresses an underexplored and well-motivated problem: lack of long-term repository memory in code localization agents, with a clear analogy to human developer expertise.
Leverages repository commit history and linked issues as a natural, underutilized source for non-parametric memory, combining episodic and semantic memory components in an intuitive way.
The proposed memory tools are simple, modular, and easily integrated into existing agentic frameworks, as demonstrated with LocAgent; appendix tool documentation and examples aid understanding.

Reports consistent improvements over strong baselines (CodeRankEmbed, Agentless, LocAgent) on SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live across Acc@1/3/5, with ablations showing both memory types contribute when combined.
Includes useful analyses: changes in tool-use behavior, per-repository correlation with available commit history, retrieval-method comparison, and per-example cost variance.
Transparently discusses failure modes, including degradation on repositories with sparse history and distraction from irrelevant retrieved memory.
The paper is clearly written and well structured, with helpful figures and tables.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: memory-augmented agents and retrieval over repository commit histories are established ideas; the proposed mechanisms are largely BM25 over commit messages plus LLM summaries of frequently edited files, with no substantially new algorithm or learning method.

Evaluation is narrow: only file-level localization is measured, not end-to-end issue resolution or patch correctness; only one backbone LLM (GPT-4o) is used, so generalization across models is unknown.
Empirical gains are modest on SWE-bench-live (+1.6 Acc@1, +3.1 Acc@5) and lack statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance analysis; the live subset is small (130 examples).
The semantic-only memory can underperform the LocAgent baseline on SWE-bench-live Acc@1 (56.9 vs. 59.2), and combined gains may not be robust across settings.

The method degrades substantially on repositories with limited commit history ('others': -13.1 Acc@5), and there is no mechanism for deciding when to rely on memory versus first-principles exploration.

Baselines and ablations are incomplete: no comparison to other memory/experience-based SE agents, no simple commit-message retrieval baseline within the same framework, and dense retrieval is tested only on django.

Reproducibility details are insufficient: prompts for generating summaries, exact custom tokenizer, commit preprocessing/filtering criteria, memory-size choices, and tool-use constraints are not fully specified or ablated.
Efficiency analysis shows average cost increases on many examples; cost-effectiveness relative to baselines is not quantified, even though memory use can add overhead and distraction.
Claims of 'significant' improvement are stronger than the evidence supports without statistical tests and end-to-end evaluation.
Data leakage/contamination safeguards are only briefly described; more rigorous validation of the filtering process would strengthen confidence.

strengths: The paper identifies the lack of long-term repository memory in code-localization agents as an important limitation, and proposes leveraging commit history as an underutilized source of repository-specific knowledge.

The design of episodic memory (past commits and linked issues) and semantic memory (summaries of frequently edited files) is intuitive and modular, making it easy to integrate into existing agentic frameworks such as LocAgent.
The experimental evaluation covers two benchmarks, SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live, with standard baselines and ablations showing that episodic and semantic memory are complementary.

The analyses on tool-usage shift, per-repository correlation with commit history, retrieval method choice, and failure modes provide useful qualitative insights into how memory changes agent behavior.
The appendix documents the memory tools and example outputs, which improves clarity and practical understanding of the proposed interfaces.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method combines existing ingredients (BM25 retrieval over commit messages, linked issues, and LLM-generated file summaries) with an existing agent framework; there is no new algorithmic or modeling contribution of the kind expected at a top-tier AI conference.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, and the claimed 'significant' improvements are modest in absolute terms (e.g., 1.6–4.9 points), while some repositories degrade substantially under the proposed method.

Baseline comparisons are narrow. The paper compares mainly against CodeRankEmbed, Agentless, and LocAgent, but does not compare against other memory-enhanced agents or commit-history-based retrieval baselines, making it hard to isolate the value of the proposed memory design.

Potential data leakage and contamination are not convincingly addressed. The filtering of overlapping issue text is vaguely described, and it is unclear whether semantic summaries are generated strictly from the base commit or could inadvertently use future code, especially given the benchmark setup.

Ablations are incomplete: there is no sensitivity analysis for the number of historical commits, the number of frequently edited files, the summary-generation model/prompt, retrieval top-k, or tool-call budgets. Memory-construction cost and latency are not reported.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper does not provide code, prompts, BM25 tokenizer details, summary-generation procedures, or exact filtering thresholds, despite relying on several non-trivial implementation choices.

The efficiency analysis is unconvincing. The cross-comparison shows increased average cost across all quadrants, not only on hard problems, and the reported costs exclude memory construction and summary generation, so the claimed strategic cost trade-off is not fully supported.

Per-repository results reveal a serious limitation: the method harms repositories with limited or irrelevant commit history (e.g., a substantial Acc@5 drop on the 'others' group), and this is not adequately addressed or mitigated.
The evaluation is only file-level localization; no line-level localization, patch generation, or end-to-end bug-fixing results are provided, limiting the practical significance of the claimed gains.

Positioning with respect to related memory-agent work is incomplete. The paper discusses some related work but does not compare experimentally or theoretically against closely related approaches such as SWE-exp or Agent Workflow Memory.

strengths: Well-motivated approach grounded in an intuitive analogy to human developers' long-term repository memory, with a clear failure-case illustration.
Introduces two complementary and practical memory mechanisms: episodic memory over past commits/issues and semantic memory over frequently edited files, both integrated modularly into LocAgent.
Evaluation spans two benchmarks (SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live) with strong baselines (CodeRankEmbed, Agentless, LocAgent), plus ablations showing both memory components contribute.
Reports consistent gains over LocAgent, e.g., Acc@5 76.5 vs. 71.6 on SWE-bench-verified and 66.2 vs. 63.1 on SWE-bench-live, with per-repository, retrieval-method, cost, and error analyses.

Provides useful practical insights, including that sparse BM25 retrieval outperforms dense retrieval for commit-message matching and that memory shifts agent behavior away from exhaustive graph traversal.
Appendix documents the memory tools and example responses, which helps clarify the interface and reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: memory-augmented agents and retrieval over repository history are existing ideas; the contribution largely adds BM25 commit search and LLM-generated file summaries as tools to an existing framework.
Evaluation is limited to file-level localization, not end-to-end bug fixing or patch generation; only GPT-4o is used, and no variance or statistical significance tests are reported.

Key hyperparameters (7,000 recent commits, top 200 frequently edited files) appear arbitrary, with no sensitivity analysis; performance degrades sharply on repositories with limited commit history (-13.1 Acc@5 on 'others').

There is a potential budget confound: memory tools enlarge the action space and increase cost on difficult examples, but there is no matched-cost or matched-step comparison to isolate the effect of memory from extra exploration.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: prompts for summary generation, BM25 tokenization details, issue-linking/crawling procedure, memory construction cost/time, and code availability are not fully specified.
The SWE-bench-live evaluation uses a filtered subset of only 130 examples, limiting generalizability, and the reported live gains are relatively small without significance testing.
Contamination filtering is described but not fully validated; linked issues and commit messages may still leak information relevant to the target issue.

strengths: Addresses a practically important limitation of repository-level coding agents: the lack of long-term repository memory, with a clear and intuitive motivation grounded in how human developers use past repository experience.

Proposes two simple, modular memory mechanisms—episodic memory of past commits/issues and semantic memory of active-file functionality—that integrate naturally into the ReAct-based LocAgent framework via well-defined tools.

Reports consistent improvements over strong baselines on both SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live, including Acc@1/3/5 gains and a downstream issue resolution-rate improvement under a patch-generation pipeline.

Provides useful ablations (episodic-only, semantic-only, full), per-repository analysis, tool-use shift analysis, cost analysis, and retrieval/tokenizer analysis, which help characterize when and why the memory helps.
Well documented appendices with tool definitions, prompt templates, examples, reproducibility statement, and plans for code release, which supports reproducibility.
Honest and informative error analysis, including the finding that repositories with sparse commit histories can suffer from distracting memory, which is important for future work.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: the memory tools largely combine existing ideas—BM25 commit retrieval, issue linking, and LLM-generated file summaries—rather than introducing a fundamentally new localization method.

Evaluation is limited to a single backbone LLM (GPT-4o), with no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals; the reported gains, especially on SWE-bench-live, could be sensitive to variance.
The SWE-bench-live evaluation uses a custom 130-example subset (intersection of lite/verified with ≤5 files), which may not be standard and limits comparability with other reported results.

Memory construction uses fixed heuristics (7,000 commits, top 200 files) chosen largely from Django-only sensitivity analysis; it is unclear how robust these choices are across repositories of different sizes, histories, and activity patterns.
Leakage control is described briefly but not rigorously validated; filtering overlapping issue text and linked commits could remove useful precedents or leave subtle leakage risks.

The retrieval ablation is mostly limited to Django and compares sparse BM25 against one dense retriever; the conclusion that sparse retrieval is generally better may not generalize across repositories or code vocabularies.

The agent has no learned or heuristic mechanism for deciding when memory is useful; the cost analysis shows increased average cost on difficult/failed examples, indicating potential distraction from irrelevant memory.
Semantic memory quality is not directly evaluated; LLM-generated file summaries may omit critical details or contain inaccuracies that propagate into localization decisions.

Downstream resolve-rate improvement is modest and assessed using the Agentless patch-generation pipeline, not an end-to-end system built around the proposed memory, so the practical impact on bug fixing remains partially indirect.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: long-term repository memory for code localization, using commit history as a natural source of past development experience.
Proposes modular episodic and semantic memory tools that can be integrated into existing agentic frameworks, demonstrated with LocAgent.
Reports experiments on SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live, with ablations for episodic/semantic memory components and analyses of tool use and cost.
Provides implementation details, appendix examples, prompts, and overhead analysis, which improves potential reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim of substantial improvement is not convincingly supported: gains are modest (Acc@5 +4.9 on SWE-bench-verified, +3.1 on SWE-bench-live), with no statistical tests, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds.

Evaluation lacks a critical control for extra compute/tool calls: the memory-augmented agent costs more, but no baseline gives LocAgent equal extra tokens/steps, so gains may come from additional exploration rather than memory.
Performance degrades significantly on repositories with limited history (others: -13.1 Acc@5), showing lack of robustness and possible negative transfer.
Technical novelty is limited: the method is essentially BM25 retrieval over commit messages plus LLM file summaries, with no learned memory, dynamic memory update, or new algorithmic insight.
Ablations are narrow: hyperparameter K and retrieval method are studied only on Django; there is no full cross-repository sensitivity, no ablation of commit window, filtering, or query generation.

Evaluation is limited to file-level localization; although the prompt mentions functions/lines, no function/line-level results are reported, and end-to-end resolution is only in the appendix with small gains.
Reference formatting/typos and missing public code at submission weaken reproducibility, and memory construction cost/scale across many repositories is not fully reported.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation in repository-level code localization: existing agents largely solve each issue from scratch without repository-specific long-term memory.
Proposes a simple but practically effective use of commit history as non-parametric memory, with complementary episodic and semantic memory components.
Introduces easy-to-integrate memory tools (SearchCommit, ExamineCommit, ViewSummary, SearchSummary) that fit naturally into agentic ReAct workflows such as LocAgent.
Reports consistent gains on SWE-bench-verified and SWE-bench-live, with ablations showing benefits from both episodic and semantic memory components.
Provides useful analyses beyond main accuracy, including agent behavior shift, API cost trade-offs, retrieval-method comparison, per-repository effects, and downstream issue-resolution impact.
Demonstrates strong reproducibility practices: public benchmarks, implementation details, prompts, documentation, and examples of memory tool outputs.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively straightforward: BM25 retrieval over commit messages and LLM summaries of frequently edited files, which may be viewed as incremental over existing agentic localization frameworks.
Evaluation is limited to file-level localization accuracy; code localization often requires function- or line-level granularity, and no such finer-grained results are reported.

Memory construction may pose contamination risks: while episodic memory filtering is described, semantic memory summary generation and source-version handling are less thoroughly validated against leakage from future commits or target fixes.
Generalization is not fully established: only GPT-4o is used as the backbone, and SWE-bench-live is restricted to a small filtered subset requiring five or fewer files.

Memory can hurt performance when history is sparse or irrelevant, as shown by the -13.1 Acc@5 drop on the 'others' repository group; the paper does not provide a robust mechanism to decide when to trust memory.

The retrieval-method ablation is conducted only on django, and hyperparameter choices such as top-K files, BM25 variants, and summary-generation prompts are not comprehensively explored across repositories.
The modularity claim is only demonstrated with LocAgent; integration with other agentic frameworks or localization pipelines is not empirically evaluated.
Semantic memory is constructed once from top-K active files and then remains static, with limited discussion of scalability, maintenance, or adaptation as codebases evolve.

Some claims of substantial improvement should be interpreted cautiously: absolute gains are moderate and vary considerably by repository, with no significance testing or confidence intervals reported.
